title: Arjuna's Question: Bow, Ask, Serve
hookLine: a student on a battlefield tells his teacher: your words confuse me
carry: the student bows, asks and serves
tomorrow: a book named for a jewel: before the guru, bring what?

cards: Any questions? Then the quiet, because nobody wants to be the one who didn't get it. So is a hard question for a teacher doubt, or respect?
On the field of Kurukshetra, a student breaks that quiet. Arjuna has just heard Krishna praise wisdom over action. In the same breath, Krishna tells him to stand up and act.

So Arjuna turns to him and says, in paraphrase from the Gita's third chapter: if you think understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible thing? Your mixed words confuse me. Tell me plainly.
A warrior, talking back to his teacher, with the armies waiting. What does the teacher do?

teach.b: He answers. No rebuke, no sigh. Krishna starts again and lays out two paths, knowing and doing, more plainly than before.
That's the pattern of the whole book. The Gita is a conversation, and Arjuna keeps asking: say it more simply, tell me who you really are, show me.

Each time, Krishna answers, and by the last chapter Arjuna says his confusion is gone. The answers worked because the questions were asked. A chapter later, the Gita names the way a student comes to a teacher.
In paraphrase, from 4.34: learn it by bowing down, by asking questions, and by serving; the wise who have seen the truth will teach you. Three words carry that verse.
Pranipata, bowing: humility before someone who knows more. Pariprashna, questioning: the kind that keeps asking until it's clear. Seva, service.
They come as a set, and each keeps the others honest.

teach.h: THE QUESTIONS ARE PART OF THE BOW.
teach.b: Bowing without questions can slide into blind obedience. Questions without bowing can turn into an argument that only wants to win. Service keeps both inside a real relationship.

This is the Hindu picture of the guru and the shishya, the student, drawn by the Gita itself. A teacher who treats every question as disloyalty has dropped one of the three. Arjuna's teacher kept answering.

how: The Bhagavad Gita (4.34) names three ways a student approaches a teacher, bowing, questioning and service, taken together; the whole Gita is set as a student's questions and a teacher's answers.

games.q: what does “modern gurus and their cautions” mean?
o: a rule against learning from any living teacher
living teachers, weighed by what old texts ask of them
the yearly fee a student pays to a guru

games.q: the Gita's student. tap the pairs.
p: bowing: humility before one who knows

s: in the Gita, Arjuna never questions Krishna
he asks again and again: say it plainly, tell me who you are, show me.
the Gita's student bows, asks and serves, as one set
4.34 joins bowing, questioning and service; each keeps the others honest.
the Gita treats a student's questions as a lack of faith
it puts questioning inside the bow, and Krishna answers every time.

games.q: a meditation teacher you admire says something in class that seems to contradict what she said last week. class ends. what fits the Gita's picture of a student?
o: let it go: asking about it would look disloyal.
ask her, respectfully, which she meant, and help stack the mats.
post a comment pointing out the contradiction for everyone.
games.why: Gita 4.34 keeps bowing, asking and serving together. Silence drops the question; the public callout drops the bow.

practice: If there's paper and a pen nearby, write down one honest question you'd bring to someone wise, about your own life, not a quiz, and not a trap. If there's no pen, say it once under your breath. Don't answer it.
Read it once, slowly, and let it sit on the page the way Arjuna's question hung in the air before the armies.

wordCard.voice: Modern gurus and their cautions. Today's caution, from the Gita: a student bows, asks and serves, all three at once.

orig.note: Sanskrit: pariprashna, questioning; the middle word of the Gita's bow, ask, serve (4.34).

carryVoice: Keep this: the student bows, asks and serves, and the questions are part of the bow. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.1–3 (Arjuna: if understanding is better than action, why urge me to this terrible deed? your mixed words confuse me; Krishna answers with two paths)
Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (learn it by bowing, by questioning, by service; the wise who have seen the truth will teach you)
Bhagavad Gita 18.73 (Arjuna: my delusion is destroyed; I stand firm, my doubts gone)
